claim: Breathing voluntarily at about six breaths a minute raises vagally mediated heart-rate variability during practice, right after one session and after multi-session training.
Slow controlled breathing is associated with greater parasympathetic activity, more alpha power and lower arousal and anxiety, though most trials are small.
Nasal breathing entrains oscillations in olfactory and limbic brain areas and improves memory and fear recognition timed to inhalation, an effect absent with mouth breathing.

The idea that a fixed stock of breaths or heartbeats sets lifespan rests on a cross-species correlation; within humans, lower resting heart rate predicts lower mortality but slowing breath has not been shown to extend life.
Reciting a rosary prayer or a yoga mantra slows breathing to about six a minute and raises baroreflex sensitivity, linking repetitive recitation to the slow-breath physiology.
Most healthy adults show a nasal cycle in which airflow alternates between the left and right nostril over hours, driven by autonomic congestion of the nasal lining.
Claims that breathing through one nostril selectively activates the opposite brain hemisphere or shifts sympathetic versus parasympathetic tone rest on small, inconsistent studies.
Meta-analysis of small randomised trials finds alternate-nostril breathing lowers blood pressure modestly, with high heterogeneity between studies.
The insula integrates signals from inside the body into a felt sense of bodily state, and disturbed interoception is implicated in anxiety, depression and eating disorders.
Experienced meditators are not reliably better than non-meditators at detecting their own heartbeats, despite reporting greater bodily awareness.
People across cultures locate distinct emotions in consistent regions of the body, suggesting feelings are partly constructed from bodily sensation.
Meditation is associated with reduced activity in the default mode network and changed coupling between it and attention and control networks, with larger effects in experienced practitioners.
Silent repetition of a single word reduces activity widely across the cortex, including default-mode regions, compared with rest.
Loss of the sense of self in deep meditation and high-dose psychedelic states takes several distinct forms and is mostly reported by very experienced meditators or at high doses.
A model holds that psychedelics relax the brain's high-level prior beliefs, letting bottom-up signals revise entrenched self-models.
A single 25 mg dose of psilocybin with psychological support reduced treatment-resistant depression scores at three weeks more than 1 mg, with adverse events in both arms.
On the predictive-processing account, perception is the brain's best guess about the causes of sensory input, constantly corrected by prediction error.
Emotion and the sense of self may arise as predictions about the body's internal state, extending predictive processing to interoception.
A theoretical account proposes that meditation progressively loosens predictive models, from reduced mind-wandering to cessation of experience in advanced states.
The gut microbiota signals to the brain through immune, endocrine and vagal routes and affects stress responses and behaviour in animals; human causal evidence is still limited.
A typical human body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells, so the body is in large part a community of other organisms.
The body replaces around 330 billion cells a day, mostly blood and gut cells, so its material is continually renewed.
People's minds wander nearly half their waking time, and they report being less happy while wandering than while focused.
Meditation programmes produce moderate improvements in anxiety, depression and pain, with low or no evidence of benefit for attention, mood or sleep beyond active controls.
Much meditation research suffers from vague definitions, small samples and overstated claims, and the evidence for its benefits is weaker than popular accounts suggest.
Meditators report a wide range of challenging experiences, including perceived lights, altered self-sense, fear and lasting distress, some needing support.
Mouse studies reported that sleep increases clearance of brain waste through the glymphatic system, but a 2024 study found clearance fell during sleep, so the claim is disputed.
Nearly every cell keeps a roughly 24-hour molecular clock entrained by light, and misalignment of these clocks is linked to metabolic and mental illness.
Intermittent fasting improves metabolic markers in animals and some humans, but trials show weight loss similar to ordinary calorie restriction.
Fasting strongly induces autophagy in animal tissues, but direct evidence that it does so in human tissues is sparse.
Ageing reflects a set of interacting cellular hallmarks such as genomic instability, loss of protein balance and stem-cell exhaustion, none yet reversed in humans.
Maximum human lifespan appears to have plateaued near 115-125 years, and radical life extension in this century is judged implausible.
Expectation and conditioning engage opioid, dopamine and prefrontal systems to produce real changes in pain and symptoms, chiefly in subjective outcomes.
Placebos given openly, with patients told they are inert, still produce moderate improvements in self-reported symptoms.
A scoping review found 220 cases of heavy-metal poisoning, mostly lead and mercury, linked to Ayurvedic and Siddha preparations, with most analysed samples over permissible limits.
About one in five Ayurvedic products bought online in the US contained detectable lead, mercury or arsenic, including rasa shastra metal preparations.
Elemental, inorganic and organic mercury are toxic to the nervous system and kidneys, and no safe therapeutic role for ingested mercury is established.
Case reports document severe poisoning, including cerebral edema, from Siddha capsules containing arsenic, mercury and lead thousands of times above safe limits.
Artemisinin, isolated from sweet wormwood after a search of traditional Chinese recipes, became a frontline malaria drug, showing traditional texts can point to real compounds.
Small randomised trials suggest ashwagandha lowers self-reported stress and anxiety, with low certainty of evidence.
Curcumin, though popular, is unstable, poorly absorbed and a frequent false positive in assays, and no double-blind trial has shown a clear therapeutic benefit.
Siddha polyherbal decoctions such as Nilavembu and Kaba Sura Kudineer have been tested in few, small COVID-19 trials, with uncertain benefit beyond standard care.
Agreement between practitioners reading the pulse in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine is low to moderate, and the methods remain poorly standardised.
Meta-analysis of morphometric studies reports modest structural brain differences in meditators across about eight regions, though small samples and publication bias are concerns.
In two combined randomised trials, eight weeks of mindfulness training produced no structural brain changes compared with active and waitlist controls.
Whether adult humans make new hippocampal neurons is disputed, with major studies reporting both near-absence and abundance.
Trained practitioners of breathing and cold exposure or of tummo meditation can voluntarily raise body temperature or modulate the innate immune response, effects once thought impossible.

Orch-OR proposes that consciousness arises from quantum computations in neuronal microtubules ending in gravity-related collapse; it remains speculative and is disputed by most physicists and neuroscientists.
Calculated decoherence times for neural quantum states are far shorter than neural processing times, a central objection to quantum-brain theories.
An underground radiation experiment ruled out the simplest parameter-free version of the gravity-related collapse model that Orch-OR depends on.
A microtubule-stabilising drug delayed isoflurane-induced unconsciousness in rats, consistent with but not proof of a microtubule role in consciousness.
Quantum cognition uses the mathematics of quantum probability to model order effects and violations of classical probability in human judgment; it makes no claim that brains are quantum devices.
Loophole-free Bell tests confirm that entangled particles show correlations no local hidden-variable theory can explain, though these cannot be used to send signals.
Mercury can be turned into gold only by nuclear reactions such as neutron bombardment of mercury isotopes, never by chemical or alchemical processing.
Reported evidence for precognition and other psychic powers failed to replicate and exposed weaknesses in standard statistical practice.
Reminders of death reliably shift people's attitudes and defence of their worldviews, a moderately sized effect across many studies, though recent large replications have been weaker.
People adapt to most gains and losses so that happiness drifts back toward a personal set point, though not fully for every life event.
The brain's dopamine 'wanting' system can drive craving independently of 'liking', so addictive desire can grow while pleasure does not.
Loving-kindness and compassion meditation improve self-reported wellbeing and reduce distress in small to moderate degree.
Indian groups descend from a mixture of ancestral populations, and widespread intermarriage gave way to strict endogamy only about 1,900 to 4,200 years ago.
